findings.summary: A word-for-word swap leaves a doubled or wrong article in the usual phrasing, so text the person running Athena reads becomes ungrammatical.
findings.evidence: The replacement for the first word is 'the person running Athena', but the preceding article is kept. The steward test title "Tell the {word} when a duty recurs" becomes "Tell the the person running Athena when a duty recurs". 'an {word}' would become 'an the person running Athena', and 'a {sandbox word}' would become 'a isolated environment'. The tests only check `contains("the person running Athena")`, so they do not catch this. A simpler fix: let the rewrite absorb a preceding 'the', 'a' or 'an' when the replacement starts with an article, or make the replacement a bare noun phrase ('person running Athena').

findings.summary: approve_request rewrites the whole request, including file and record content copied in as evidence, so quoted source text is quietly changed.
findings.evidence: `plain_boundary_text(&out)` runs over the full rendered request, which embeds the content of cited files and records. A cited line that uses one of the listed words in an unrelated sense (the 'lease' word becomes 'claim') reaches the reader changed, with no marker that it was rewritten. Admission would refuse it otherwise, so this is a reasonable trade-off. A note in the request saying quoted text was reworded would keep it honest.

findings.summary: Redundant double sanitising in the error-review path.
findings.evidence: root_cause_request_at already ends with `plain_boundary_text(&request)`, and try_error_review applies `.and_then(|text| plain_boundary_text(&text))` to the same text again. Harmless, but a reader may wonder which call is the real one.

findings.summary: The replacement table is separate from boundary_words, so the two lists can drift apart; a test catches this.
findings.evidence: The 17-entry table repeats the fragments of boundary_words. The test plain_boundary_text_rewrites_every_listed_word_and_fragment loops over boundary_words(), so a newly listed word with no replacement would fail it. That is acceptable, though one table holding both the word and its replacement would remove the duplication.

summary: The change passes. It adds one shared check, `plain_boundary_text`, in athena-context/briefs.rs. The check is built on `boundary_scan`, `boundary_words` and `boundary_fragments`, rewrites each boundary word to plain wording and scans the result again. It is called by every writer the request lists: `StewardRequest::new`, `validate_item` and `check_key` in steward.rs; `root_cause_request_at` and `try_error_review` in hestia.rs; `apply_answer` in introspect.rs; and `approve_request` in work_decisions.rs. Several other Hestia and code-health writers build their requests through `StewardRequest::new`, so they are covered too. I ran the five new writer tests and the three helper tests, and all pass. The approve-work test first shows the unmodified text is refused at admission, then shows approve_work succeeds and the stored request is clean. The repository policy scan also passes, so no tracked file holds a boundary word. Athena's recorded fmt, clippy and test runs all passed. All six changed files are on the deliverables list. The main weakness: a plain word-for-word swap leaves bad grammar in the usual case. "Tell the <word>" becomes "Tell the the person running Athena", and the tests do not catch it.
